title: Netflow and IPFIX
summary: NetFlow and its open equivalent IPFIX are flow-export technologies that summarise network conversations rather than capturing every packet. A router or switch observes packets, groups them into flows keyed by source and destination address, ports, protocol and other fields, and periodically exports records that describe each flow with counters, timestamps and interface information. Because exports are aggregated, the storage and bandwidth cost is a small fraction of full packet capture, which makes it practical to retain flow data for weeks or months across an entire estate. That retention is the core defensive value. Flow records answer who talked to whom, when, how much and over which port, and they stay useful for retrospective investigation long after the packets are gone. Common analytical uses include detecting exfiltration by volume and direction, identifying beaconing through regular inter-arrival patterns, mapping external exposure during incident scoping, and proving that a segmentation policy is genuinely enforced. Flow data is deliberately lossy: it carries no payload, so it cannot confirm what was transferred or match content signatures, and sampling, aggregation timeouts and top-talker reporting on the exporting device all reduce fidelity. Adversaries and ordinary applications can tunnel over permitted protocols, so flow analysis often produces the hypothesis that packet capture or endpoint telemetry must confirm. Practical deployments must handle clock synchronisation, because flow timestamps are useless for correlation when devices disagree, asymmetric routing so both directions are collected, collector capacity and duplicate exports, and consistent interface naming so that a flow can be tied to a physical or logical path. Enrichment with asset inventory, geolocation and threat intelligence turns raw records into something an analyst can prioritise, and keeping flow data beside DNS, proxy and authentication logs resolves most incidents that no single source could explain.
objectives: You will be able to describe how flows are defined, aggregated and exported and what fidelity that costs.
You will be able to triage flow records for beaconing, exfiltration volume and unexpected lateral movement.
You will be able to design a collector pipeline that handles time sync, asymmetry and duplicates.
You will be able to enrich flow data with asset, geolocation and reputation context for prioritisation.
You will be able to test a segmentation policy against observed flow evidence rather than documentation.
You will be able to state when flow metadata is insufficient and packet or endpoint evidence is required.

beginner.definition: NetFlow and IPFIX are ways for network devices to summarise traffic instead of recording every packet. The device groups packets into flows, which are conversations between two addresses, and sends a short record for each one. A record says who talked to whom, when, for how long and how much data moved.
beginner.whyItMatters: Full packet capture is expensive to store, so most teams keep only a few days of it. Flow records are tiny, so you can keep months of them and still answer questions later. When something goes wrong, flows show you which machines spoke to a strange address and how much data left. They will not tell you what was inside the traffic, but they point you to where to look next.
howItWorks: A router or switch watches the packets that pass through it every second.
It groups packets with the same addresses, ports and protocol into one flow.
It counts bytes and packets for that flow and notes the start and end time.
Every minute or so it exports those records to a collector, which stores them.
Analysts then search the records for odd patterns, such as regular small transfers at night.
Enriching records with asset names and known bad addresses makes them easier to rank.
beginner.example: Think of your monthly phone bill. It lists every call: the number dialled, the date, the duration and sometimes the data used. It does not record what you said. That is exactly what a flow record is. If someone made many short calls to the same strange number at three in the morning, the bill would show the pattern clearly. Flow data works the same way and is far cheaper to keep than recordings.
takeaways: Flow records summarise conversations; they never contain the content.
Because they are small, you can keep them for months and look back.
Regular small transfers to one address often mean hidden beaconing.
